title: People Often Express Content Conflict Relationally
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post is the mirror image of the previous one on conflict. Admired Leadership argues that when people feel their influence is diminished, because they cannot win the argument or are upstaged by better ideas, they attack the person rather than the substance. They avoid the colleague, claim a personality clash and say the other is not their cup of tea. The author contends that such so-called personality clashes can keep conflicts alive for years because even the aggrieved party often does not recognize the real cause. Leaders are urged to make this their first hypothesis and to help the parties reach more parity of influence.
points: When people lose influence in a debate, they often recast a content disagreement as a personal dislike.
Many long-running personality clashes are really contests over influence that no one has named.
Even the person who feels diminished often does not recognize what is driving the conflict.
Leaders should treat influence imbalance as their first conclusion when two colleagues dislike each other.
Giving both parties more parity of influence usually cools the conflict and allows a more harmonious relationship.
quotes: When people don’t have the influence they would like, can’t win the argument, or get upstaged by superior ideas or advocacy, they take issue with the person, not the substance. In other words, they express conflict over content relationally.

They avoid those people, listen but refrain from engaging, say their personalities clash, tell others the other party bothers them or is not their cup of tea, and create a general feeling of dislike for the other party.
This pattern is quite common, yet often goes unrecognized even by the party who feels substantively inadequate or diminished.
This makes working through the conflict nearly impossible, which is why so many so-called personality clashes sometimes keep the fires of conflict going between colleagues for years.

The tendency for people to express content conflict through dissatisfaction about the relationship is so strong it should become a leader’s first conclusion when trying to understand why two colleagues have such distaste for each other.
Just understanding what is really going on is enough to help leaders manage the conflict and not fall into the trap of attending to the wrong issue.
